bib.title: LongCite: Enabling LLMs to Generate Fine-grained Citations in Long-context QA

legacy_report:
SOURCE: LongCite: Enabling LLMs to Generate Fine-grained Citations in Long-context QA. Jiajie Zhang, Yushi Bai, Xin Lv, Wanjun Gu, Danqing Liu, Minhao Zou, Shulin Cao, Lei Hou, Yuxiao Dong, Ling Feng, Juanzi Li (Tsinghua, Zhipu AI). arXiv 2409.02897v3, preprint, 10 Sep 2024.

COVERAGE: 78,490 chars, 24 pages. Read the body, the results tables, the appendices (model cards, case studies, evaluation cost) and the prompt figures 10-13 in full. I skimmed the reference list, and I only skimmed the Figure 4-9 judge prompts, which are boilerplate. The extraction is clean. The full text is at /tmp/longcite.txt (line numbers below refer to it). There is no Limitations section.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Current LLMs cite poorly when asked to answer and cite in one pass over a long context. Proprietary models reach citation F1 of about 0.5 on two datasets, and their citations are coarser than a 128-token chunk.
  number: GPT-4o citation length 220 (about 6 sentences per citation); Table 2 averages 65.6 (GPT-4o), 67.2 (Claude-3-sonnet), 65.4 (GLM-4)
  setup: LongBench-Cite, LAC-S strategy (full context with numbered sentences, one-shot prompt), GPT-4o as judge
  quote: "The citation F1 of proprietary LLMs on LongBench-chat and HotpotQA is only around 0.5, which means less than half statements in their responses are fully supported by the citations." and "the citation length of GPT-4o reaches 220 and each cited snippet contains about 6 sentences on average."
  where: p.5, lines 268-273

- claim: Open-source models cite much worse than proprietary models, mostly because of format errors and failure to find evidence.
  number: avg citation F1 27.2 (GLM-4-9B-chat), 19.7 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), 40.4 (Llama-3.1-70B), 51.5 (Mistral-Large)
  setup: same as above
  quote: "open-source models often generate citations that do not conform to the prescribed format; (2) relatively weak evidence-searching ability: they often fail to find evidence for some statements (i.e., Ci = ∅), or only find partially supporting or irrelevant evidence."
  where: p.5, Table 2 and lines 261-267

- claim: Asking for citations in the same pass through in-context learning lowers answer correctness relative to plain long-context QA.
  number: GPT-4o correctness ratio (CR) 88%, GLM-4 95%, Llama-3.1-8B 86%
  setup: LongBench-Cite, Table 3, CR = C / C_LQA × 100%
  quote: "generating responses and citations at once through in-context learning always leads to correctness degradation due to the distribution shift from the post-training data."
  where: p.6, Table 3

- claim: The CoF post-hoc pipeline (generate the answer first, retrieve chunks, add chunk citations, extract sentence spans, filter) keeps correctness at 100% and gives the best citation F1 among post-hoc methods. One-pass methods score higher on citation F1 but lose correctness.
  number: CoF F1 65.8, CL 89, CR 100%; post-LC-S 57.3 F1; post-RC-C 63.8; post-RC-S 62.8 (CL 48); LAC-S 65.4 (CR 95%); RAC-S 79.1 F1 but CR 79%; RAC-C 72.5 F1, CR 87%
  setup: GLM-4 as backbone, Zhipu Embedding-2 retriever, lmax=10, k=40, 128-token chunks, LongBench-Cite (Table 4)
  quote: "though attaining higher citation F1, one-pass methods typically generate answers with lower correctness, failing to fully leverage LLMs' long-context QA capacities."
  where: p.7-8, Table 4, lines 450-464

- claim: Retrieving before citing (post-RC) beats searching the whole context (post-LC) for citation F1. Extracting sentences from the cited chunks beats chunk-level citation.
  number: post-LC-C 47.3 vs post-RC-C 63.8 vs CoF 65.8 F1
  setup: Table 4, GLM-4
  quote: "post-hoc retrieval-based methods (i.e., post-RC-C, post-RC-S and CoF) benefit from a more focused evidence search space, typically yielding better performance."
  where: p.8, line 458

- claim: SFT on the 44.6k citation examples (LongCite-8B/9B) gives the best citation quality, ahead of GPT-4o, Claude-3-sonnet and GLM-4, with finer granularity.
  number: avg citation F1 72.0 (8B) and 69.2 (9B) vs 65.6 GPT-4o; citation length 85 and 91 vs 220; F1 gains over GPT-4o of 6.4 and 3.6
  setup: LongBench-Cite, LAC-S one-shot prompt, GPT-4o judge; base models Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B; 4,000 steps (about 2 epochs, 18 h), batch 8, lr 1e-5, 4 nodes × 8 H800
  quote: "LongCite-8B/9B improves the overall citation F1 by 6.4/3.6, 4.8/2.0, and 6.6/3.8, respectively."
  where: p.9, lines 522-526, Table 2

- claim: The trained models beat the CoF pipeline that made their data, which hints at self-improvement.
  number: 72.0 and 69.2 vs 65.8
  quote: "LongCite-8B and LongCite-9B even attain higher citation F1 than the data construction pipeline CoF (72.0 and 69.2 v.s. 65.8), implying a potential for continuous self-improvement."
  where: p.9

- claim: Training with citations raises answer correctness compared to plain long-context SFT, so citation training helps rather than costs.
  number: CR 107% (8B), 109% (9B); correctness up "16%/28%" over LongSFT-8B/9B (avg C 71.7 vs C_LQA 67.6; 70.4 vs 65.6)
  setup: LongSFT-8B/9B are trained on the same QA pairs without citations. Table 3, five datasets plus LongBench-Chat.
  quote: "the correctness of LongCite-8B/9B increased by 16%/28% over LongSFT-8B/9B."
  where: p.9, Table 3

- claim: The authors give two reasons for the correctness gain, based on manual comparison of three cases. Citations help the model find evidence and so reduce hallucination. They also let it use the context more uniformly, where LongSFT models over-use the head of the context.
  number: none (qualitative, 3 case studies in Tables 9-11)
  quote: "LongSFT models tend to use more information from the head part of the context and only roughly utilize or even ignore the rest of the context."
  where: p.9, Tables 9-11

- claim: Ablations on LongBench-Chat with LongCite-9B. Citation-free SFT cannot cite. Removing the filter hurts precision. Data built with post-RAC-S is much worse, because retrieved sentences give discontinuous citation numbers such as [3][7][15].
  number: LongCite-9B R 57.6 / P 78.1 / F1 63.6 / CL 112 / C 67.6; standard SFT F1 6.3; no filtering F1 61.2 (P 71.2); post-RAC-S data F1 50.1
  setup: Table 5, LongBench-Chat only
  quote: "post-RAC-S directly recalls sentences that are not necessarily adjacent from the context, resulting in many discontinuous citation numbers (such as [3][7][15]...), which makes subsequent training difficult."
  where: p.9-10, Table 5

- claim: Citation quality and correctness rise together.
  number: none (Figure 3, three correctness bins)
  quote: "responses with higher correctness typically have higher citation qualities, demonstrating a mutually promoting relationship between these two attributes."
  where: p.10

- claim: The GPT-4o judge for citation quality agrees with humans much better than the ALCE NLI judge (TRUE). Humans score higher than GPT-4o in absolute terms.
  number: kappa 0.655 (precision) vs 0.146 for ALCE; recall kappa 0.593 (partial counted as unsupported) vs 0.247; accuracy 88.8 vs 47.4 (precision), 75.0 vs 64.7 (recall)
  setup: human annotation of 150 responses, 1,064 statements, 909 citations from GLM-4, LongCite-8B and LongCite-9B on LongBench-Chat
  quote: "the Cohen's kappa coefficients between GPT-4o and human are significantly higher compared to ALCE (Table 7), demonstrating a substantial agreement for citation recall (0.593 when treating "partially support" as "not support" following ALCE) and citation precision (0.655)."
  where: p.10, Tables 6-7

- claim: The data filter drops any instance where under 20% of statements carry citations, on the reasoning that such answers lean on parametric knowledge and risk hallucination. 50k source documents became 44,600 instances.
  number: 20%; 44,600; 128-token chunks; up to 128k-token contexts
  quote: "we discard the instance if less than 20% of the statements in the answer have citations."
  where: p.7-8

- claim: Evaluation cost per run of LongBench-Cite with the GPT-4o judge.
  number: about $4 for correctness, about $25 for citation quality
  quote: "a run of GPT-4o evaluation for correctness/citation quality costs about $4/$25."
  where: Appendix D, p.15

METRIC DEFINITIONS (for the note)
- Citation recall is scored 0 / 0.5 / 1 per statement, judged on the concatenated cited snippets. A statement with no citation gets 1 if it is a "functional" sentence (intro, transition, summary), otherwise 0.
- Citation precision is 0/1 per citation. A snippet counts as relevant if it at least partially supports the statement.
- F1 is the harmonic mean of the two.
- Citation length is the average tokens per cited snippet. The authors use it to stop gaming F1 by citing the whole context.
- Correctness ratio is CR = C / C_LQA × 100%.

LIMITS
- There is no Limitations section.
- The authors note that GPT-4o judge scores run lower than human scores because cited snippets contain unresolved pronouns ("he/she", "our method"). They suggest anaphora resolution but say it would raise cost.
- Coarser citation granularity gives an unfair advantage on recall and precision. They use this to explain the gap on GovReport, where GLM-4 has CL 188 against 86 for LongCite-9B and LongCite scores lower.
- Context is capped at 128k tokens. The benchmark is about 1,250 examples across 6 datasets, and LongBench-Chat has only 50 queries. Most ablations use LongBench-Chat alone.
- The scope is long-context QA with the whole document in the prompt. Retrieval-based one-pass citing (RAC) was only tested with GLM-4, not as a trained RAG system. They say RAG "often leads to compromised answer quality due to incomplete context information", but RAC-S still scored the highest citation F1 (79.1) while losing correctness.
- The evaluation is GPT-4o-judged. Nothing in the paper tests the judge on the paper's own training data.
- The data is synthetic (GLM-4 self-instruct questions, GLM-4 citations). There is no human check of the training set.
- Dated: models are GPT-4o-2024-05-13, Claude-3-sonnet, GLM-4-0520, Llama-3.1. Newer models and native citation APIs are not covered.
- Citations are sentence-number spans over a pre-numbered context, which is a different format from RAG with chunk IDs.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Gao et al. 2023b (ALCE: "Enabling large language models to generate text with citations"): citation recall/precision, chunk-level citations, the TRUE NLI judge (Honovich et al. 2022).
- Nakano et al. 2021 (WebGPT), Menick et al. 2022, Bohnet et al. 2022 (attributed QA), Gao et al. 2023a (RARR). These are the web-page-level and post-hoc citation approaches.
- Wang et al. 2023 (Self-Instruct) for QA generation.
- Bai et al. 2023 (LongBench), Bai et al. 2024 (LongAlign: GPT-4o correctness scoring, query generation, packing with loss weighting).
- Data and models: Yang et al. 2018 (HotpotQA), He et al. 2018 (DuReader), Huang et al. 2021 (GovReport), Zeng et al. 2024 (GLM-4), Vavekanand & Sam 2024 (Llama 3.1), Shoeybi et al. 2019 (Megatron-LM), Chiang et al. 2023 (ShareGPT / Vicuna).
- Contemporaneous: Huang et al. 2024 (fine-grained grounded citations), cited for the point that coarse granularity hurts user experience.

CODE: none in the paper (repo: https://github.com/THUDM/LongCite). Prompt formats worth keeping, from Figure 10, p.21:
- Output format: "<statement>{S}<cite>[{s1}-{e1}][{s2}-{e2}]...</cite></statement>"
- "For other sentences such as introductory sentences, summarization sentences, reasoning, and inference, you still need to append "<cite></cite>" to them to indicate they need no citations."
- The context is sentence-numbered as "<C0>{Sentence 0} <C1>{Sentence 1} ...".
- The Figure 13 extraction prompt tells the model to output "No relevant information" when the passage supports nothing.

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p.3): chunk-level vs sentence-level citations, with the same OWRA statement cited as [7] versus [22-23]. It shows why chunk citations cut off sentences.
- Figure 2 (p.6): the four-stage CoF pipeline (self-instruct, chunk citations, sentence extraction, filter at 20%). It is the clearest summary of the method.
- Figure 3 (p.9): citation F1 by correctness bin.
- Tables 2-5 hold the key numbers. Table 4 is the strategy comparison: LAC/RAC/post-hoc, chunk vs sentence.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The intro says "We introduce LongBench-Chat" among the contributions, where the benchmark is LongBench-Cite (a typo in the paper). The Table 2 column header text is garbled by extraction. In the Table 4 header, the "C" values for some rows are in a different order from the header text, so check the layout in the PDF before quoting per-dataset cells. Averages and CR are reliable. Table 3 lists Avg first and then per-dataset triples. The text says the post-RC-S citation length is 49 against CoF's 89, while Table 4 shows 48.0, a small mismatch.
